::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` the superb lyrebird of south-eastern Australia is one of the best [vocal mimics]{.hl} known. About 80% of a male's song is made of imitations of other species, mostly other birds, and the imitations are remarkably accurate.

_Sources: Wildlife Victoria; Dalziell et al. (2012), Animal Behaviour_
:::

## Who I am

I am Dr Massimiliano Canzi, [Max]{.hl} for short.

. . .

I studied linguistics in [Milan]{.hl} (BA), [Manchester]{.hl} (MA) and [York]{.hl} (MSc), and returned to [Manchester]{.hl} for my PhD.

. . .

I work on how listeners [perceive]{.hl} speech and how speakers [produce]{.hl} it, mostly with experiments and quantitative methods. Forensic speech science is one of my interests.

## Who are you?

Tell us briefly:

- Your [name]{.hl} and your [programme]{.hl}
- How much [phonetics]{.hl} you have done so far
- A forensic case involving [speech]{.hl} or [language]{.hl} that you have heard of, in the news, in a podcast or on TV
- One thing you would like to [take away]{.hl} from this course

# The course

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` female superb lyrebirds also [sing]{.hl} and mimic, especially when defending their nests, when they imitate predators and alarm calls. Their songs were long overlooked: adult females look almost identical to young males, so singing females were easily taken for males.

_Source: Dalziell & Welbergen (2016), Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution_
:::

Leemann, A., Perkins, R., Sullivan Buker, G., & Foulkes, P. (2024). _An Introduction to Forensic Phonetics and Forensic Linguistics_. Routledge.

. . .

- Real [cases]{.hl}, [exercises]{.hl} and suggestions for further reading in every chapter

## Exercises

The book has exercises in every chapter, and we do many of them together.

. . .

- In forensic work there is often [no single correct answer]{.hl}
- What matters is how you get to your answer, and how [sure]{.hl} you can be
- Do the exercises before you read the solutions: this field is learnt by [doing]{.hl}

## What this course is, and is not

- A [grounding]{.hl} in the methods and problems of forensic speech science
- A first step towards [further study]{.hl}: forensic phoneticians train for years, at postgraduate level and in forensic labs
- [Not]{.hl} a qualification to do casework

. . .

The same holds for the book, as its authors point out.

# Forensic phonetics and linguistics

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` a lyrebird raised in captivity in New South Wales in the 1920s is said to have learnt [flute tunes]{.hl} and passed them on to wild lyrebirds after its release. Flute-like songs can still be heard there, but recordings made over 40 years suggest that the local song has been stable, not newly learnt.

_Sources: Powys, Taylor & Probets (2013), Environmental Humanities; Probets, Taylor & Powys (2020), Corella_
:::

## Two fields

- [Forensic phonetics]{.hl}: speech and voices as evidence. Who is speaking? What was said? Is a recording genuine?
- [Forensic linguistics]{.hl}: language as evidence. Who wrote a text? What does it mean? How is language used in police interviews and courts?

. . .

Despite the names, few practitioners work in [both]{.hl}. Most specialise further, so casework is often done by [teams]{.hl}.

## Where the fields meet

- [Language analysis in the asylum procedure]{.hl} (LAAP): where does an asylum seeker's speech suggest they grew up? (session 7)
- [Record keeping]{.hl}, [report writing]{.hl} and acting as an [expert witness]{.hl}: the same principles apply in both fields, and in all forensic sciences (session 8)

## You do it every day

When you answer the phone, you analyse the first few words, usually without noticing:

- Do I know this [voice]{.hl}?
- Does it match the [name]{.hl} on the screen?
- Is the caller [young or old]{.hl}, [local or not]{.hl}, [calm or upset]{.hl}?

. . .

Forensic phonetics asks the same questions, [systematically]{.hl}, and asks how reliable the answers are.

## An old idea: shibboleth

> And the Gileadites took the passages of Jordan before the Ephraimites: and it was so, that when those Ephraimites which were escaped said, Let me go over; that the men of Gilead said unto him, Art thou an Ephraimite? If he said, Nay; Then said they unto him, Say now Shibboleth: and he said Sibboleth: for he could not frame to pronounce it right.

_Judges 12:5–6, King James Bible_

. . .

A crude [speaker profile]{.hl}: /ʃ/ for Gileadites, /s/ for Ephraimites.

## A recent shibboleth

- In 2022, Ukrainians reportedly asked strangers to say [паляниця]{.hl} (_palianytsia_, a kind of bread) to unmask Russian saboteurs (Hyde, 2022)
- The word was believed to be hard to pronounce for speakers of Russian
- _Shibboleth_ itself is now an everyday word for any sign of group membership

## Discussion

Is the pronunciation of [one word]{.hl} enough to tell where someone is from?

. . .

- What else could explain the "wrong" pronunciation?
- What if the speaker [knows]{.hl} the test?
- What happens if the test gets it wrong?

. . .

The book's answer, and ours: [no]{.hl}. One word is never enough for serious legal decisions. Session 3 shows how profiling is done instead.

## No two samples are the same

```{r vowels-sim, fig.height = 4.4}
set.seed(27)
vowel_means <- tibble(
  vowel = c("FLEECE", "TRAP", "PALM"),
  f1 = c(290, 720, 640), f2 = c(2250, 1560, 1080)
)
sim_vowels <- function(speaker, recording, f1_shift, f2_shift, n = 15) {
  vowel_means |>
    mutate(data = map2(f1, f2, \(a, b) tibble(F1 = rnorm(n, a + f1_shift, a * 0.07),
                                             F2 = rnorm(n, b + f2_shift, b * 0.05)))) |>
    select(vowel, data) |>
    unnest(data) |>
    mutate(speaker = speaker, recording = recording)
}
vowels <- bind_rows(
  sim_vowels("Speaker A", "Speaker A, recording 1", 0, 0),
  sim_vowels("Speaker A", "Speaker A, recording 2", 15, -40),
  sim_vowels("Speaker B", "Speaker B", 50, 120)
)
ggplot(vowels, aes(F2, F1, colour = recording)) +
  stat_ellipse(level = 0.68, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.55, size = 1.8) +
  geom_text(data = vowel_means, aes(f2, f1, label = vowel), inherit.aes = FALSE,
            colour = mist, size = 5, nudge_y = -95) +
  scale_x_reverse() +
  scale_y_reverse() +
  labs(x = "F2 (Hz)", y = "F1 (Hz)", colour = NULL)
```

Simulated vowels: the same speaker never says a vowel twice the same way, and different speakers [overlap]{.hl}.

# Beware the CSI effect

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` lyrebirds are famous for imitating [chainsaws]{.hl} and other machines. But the well-known recordings come from captive birds, such as one at Adelaide Zoo: as of 2014, no recording was known of a wild lyrebird mimicking a mechanical sound.

_Source: Taylor (2014), The Conversation_
:::

## Forensic science on TV

- Experts collect samples, interview suspects and analyse everything, alone
- Results arrive in [seconds]{.hl}, from impressive software
- Conclusions are a [match]{.hl} or a [mismatch]{.hl}, "with 99.4% certainty"
- A "[voiceprint]{.hl}" on screen matches a stored sample perfectly

## Forensic science in reality

- Analyses take [days]{.hl}, not seconds
- Experts rarely, if ever, report "match" or "mismatch": there is almost always some [doubt]{.hl}
- [Objectivity]{.hl} and [transparency]{.hl} matter more than speed
- No two samples of speech are ever identical, so there is no such thing as a voice "match"

## Even DNA is not a "match"

- A DNA sample from a crime scene is [identical]{.hl} to the suspect's DNA
- This does not mean the suspect committed the crime: it means they [could]{.hl} have
- So could everyone else who shares that profile, possibly [thousands]{.hl} of people
- Other evidence (where the suspect was, a motive) is for the [court]{.hl}, not for the forensic scientist

## Two propositions

The expert weighs the evidence under two competing [propositions]{.hl}:

- [Prosecution]{.hl}: the two samples come from the [same]{.hl} source
- [Defence]{.hl}: the two samples come from [different]{.hl} sources

. . .

The question is not "are they the same?", but: how much more likely is the evidence under one proposition than under the other? More in sessions 4 and 8.

## Similar is not enough

```{r typicality, fig.height = 4.2}
f0_mean <- 115
f0_sd <- 20
cases <- tibble(case = c("Case 1", "Case 2"), offender = c(116, 72), suspect = c(118, 74))
share <- function(x) pnorm(x + 5, f0_mean, f0_sd) - pnorm(x - 5, f0_mean, f0_sd)
cases <- mutate(cases, share = share(offender))
curve_df <- tibble(f0 = seq(45, 185, by = 0.5), density = dnorm(f0, f0_mean, f0_sd))
ggplot(curve_df, aes(f0, density)) +
  geom_area(fill = dim_col) +
  geom_line(colour = muted, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(data = cases, aes(xintercept = offender, colour = case), linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(data = cases, aes(xintercept = suspect, colour = case), linewidth = 1.2, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_text(data = cases, aes(x = offender, y = 0.0215, label = case, colour = case),
            size = 5.5, hjust = 1.15) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Case 1" = kingfisher, "Case 2" = hornbill)) +
  labs(x = "Mean F0 of the speaker (Hz)", y = "Speakers in the population") +
  theme(legend.position = "none", axis.text.y = element_blank())
```

Simulated mean F0 of adult male speakers. Solid: offender. Dashed: suspect.

## Similar is not enough

In both cases, the offender and the suspect differ by only [2 Hz]{.hl}. But:

- Case 1: about [`r round(cases$share[1] * 100)`%]{.hl} of speakers have a mean F0 within 5 Hz of the offender's
- Case 2: only about [`r round(cases$share[2] * 100, 1)`%]{.hl} do

. . .

The same similarity is much stronger evidence when the feature is [rare]{.hl}. Experts call this [typicality]{.hl}: it matters as much as similarity.

## Discussion

A TV expert says: "The voices match, with [99.4% certainty]{.hl}."

- What could the 99.4% possibly mean?
- What information would you need to judge it?
- Who should decide whether the suspect is guilty?

# Working with forensic data

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` while courting, a male superb lyrebird imitates a whole [mobbing flock]{.hl}: the alarm calls of several species harassing a predator. He does it when a female tries to leave and during mating, although no predator is around: an acoustic illusion that may keep her from leaving.

_Source: Dalziell et al. (2021), Current Biology_
:::

## What the data can be like

- Much forensic material is [mundane]{.hl}: phone calls about financial transactions, for example
- Some is [distressing]{.hl}: threats, violence, recordings of crimes
- The context of a case can be disturbing even when the recording itself is not

## Looking after yourself

Giménez, Elstein & Queralt (2020) interviewed forensic linguists about their wellbeing. Three themes stood out:

- [Graphic content]{.hl}
- [Pressure]{.hl}
- [Personal experiences]{.hl} that a case brings back

. . .

- It is always fine to set [boundaries]{.hl}, take a break, or skip material you cannot face today
- How serious a crime is says nothing about how much a case will affect you
- Do not struggle in silence: the university's counselling service, and I, are there to help

## Remember the victims

- Many people know the names of notorious criminals; far fewer know the names of their [victims]{.hl}
- This gives perpetrators notoriety and takes attention away from the people they harmed
- In 2019, New Zealand's Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern refused to name the man who attacked two mosques in Christchurch

. . .

Our analyses often focus on the person who produced the speech, often the perpetrator. Keep the [people harmed]{.hl} in mind.

## How we talk about cases

- The words we use about crimes and the people involved carry [power]{.hl}
- Dark humour can be a way of coping, but you never know who is listening: a victim's or an offender's family member could be in the room
- Language around these topics keeps changing: we keep learning

## Ethics

- Know the [limits]{.hl} of your expertise and of your methods, and never comment beyond them
- Be [objective]{.hl}: no conclusion should be stronger or weaker than the analysis supports
- Do not try to help [either side]{.hl}: the expert assists the court
- A person accused of a crime is presumed [innocent]{.hl}: if the evidence leaves doubt, the court must know

. . .

Staying impartial is perhaps the hardest skill in the job, and it is learnt through experience, under the guidance of experienced practitioners.

## Further resources

- [IAFPA](https://www.iafpa.net/): the International Association for Forensic Phonetics and Acoustics
- [IAFLL](https://iafll.org/): the International Association for Forensic and Legal Linguistics
- _International Journal of Speech, Language and the Law_
- Nolan, McDougall & Hudson (eds.) (2024), _The Oxford Handbook of Forensic Phonetics_
- [Forensic Transcription Australia](https://forensictranscription.com.au/): Helen Fraser's site on transcripts of covert recordings

## Summary

::: {.takeaway}
- Forensic phonetics treats [speech]{.hl} as evidence; forensic linguistics treats [language]{.hl} as evidence
- No two speech samples are identical: experts weigh [similarities]{.hl} and [differences]{.hl}, never declare a "match"
- Similarity counts only together with [typicality]{.hl}
- The expert assists the court, [objectively]{.hl}, within the limits of their expertise
- The material can be hard: look after yourself, and remember the people behind the cases
:::
